# Code review iteration

Reviewed the full first-party source of github.com/kamilsk/grafaman at commit `3e0d02d 2020-12-08`: `main.go`, all packages under `internal/` (cmd, cnf, model, presenter, progress, provider/grafana, provider/graphite, provider/graphite/cache, repl), `tools/`, plus `go.mod`, `Makefile`, `.travis.yml`, `.golangci.yml`, `.goreleaser.yml`, and `README.md`. Vendor tree, `.github/issues/`, and `.github/roadmap/` were excluded. Review angle: real defects first (correctness, concurrency, security), then idiomaticity against 2026 Go practice, then repo-wide currency consolidated into a single modernization finding. No previous files existed in `.github/reviews/`, so nothing was matched against.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Racy return statement can silently drop fetched metrics

`internal/provider/graphite/provider.go:106`

```go
return metrics, group.Wait()
```

`recursive` spawns goroutines (line 87) that append to the shared `metrics` slice under a mutex (lines 98–100), reassigning the local slice variable on growth. The return statement then reads `metrics` in the same expression that calls `group.Wait()`. The Go spec does not order a plain operand read relative to a function call in the same return statement, so the slice header can be (and under gc, is) copied *before* `Wait` returns. Every append that reallocates the backing array after that copy is lost from the returned value even though `Wait` dutifully blocks for it, and `go test -race` flags the unsynchronized read. The practical symptom is the worst kind: an occasionally incomplete metrics list — for a coverage-reporting tool, silently wrong numbers.

**Fix.** Split the return so the read is sequenced after the synchronization point: `if err := group.Wait(); err != nil { return nil, err }; return metrics, nil`. Apply the same pattern anywhere else a value guarded by `errgroup` is returned alongside `Wait()`.

## 2. HTTP status codes are never checked so a 404 becomes a fake report

`internal/provider/grafana/provider.go:88` (also `internal/provider/graphite/provider.go:143`)

Both providers go straight from `client.Do` to `json.NewDecoder(response.Body).Decode(...)` without ever looking at `response.StatusCode`. Grafana answers an unknown dashboard UID with `404 {"message":"Dashboard not found"}`; that body decodes cleanly into the payload struct, leaving `payload.Dashboard` zero-valued. The tool then proceeds with an empty query set and prints a confident 0.00% coverage report with exit code 0 — a silently wrong result for a typo in `-d`. The Graphite side is only marginally better: an HTML 4xx/5xx page surfaces as a cryptic "decode metrics fetch response" JSON error with no status or body context. The retry policy (`strategy.NetworkError`) also never retries 5xx responses because a non-nil response is not a network error, so transient server errors fail on the first attempt while the retry machinery sits idle.

**Fix.** After a successful `Do`, require `response.StatusCode == http.StatusOK`; otherwise read a bounded body snippet and return an error carrying status and URL. Optionally classify 5xx as retryable inside the `what` closure (return a typed retryable error and drain/close the body between attempts) so the retry stack does something useful.

## 3. Graphite from parameter uses Go duration syntax that Graphite rejects

`internal/provider/graphite/provider.go:59`

```go
q.Add(fromParam, fmt.Sprintf("now-%s", last))
```

`last` is a `time.Duration`, so the default `--last 24h` serializes as `now-24h0m0s`. Graphite's at-time grammar (graphite-web and graphite-api, the API this file's doc comment links to) accepts units `s|min|h|d|w|mon|y` and raises "Invalid offset unit 'm'" for the bare `m` in `0m0s` — every request with the default flags gets a 500 from a vanilla Graphite. It presumably worked in production only because carbonapi's parser tolerates `m` as minutes. Combined with [[#2. HTTP status codes are never checked so a 404 becomes a fake report]], the user sees an unrelated JSON decode error instead of the real cause.

**Fix.** Serialize the offset in universally supported units: `fmt.Sprintf("now-%ds", int(last/time.Second))` (and validate `last > 0`). Add a unit test pinning the emitted query string.

## 4. Progress bar renders to stdout and is never shut down

`internal/progress/progress.go:29`

```go
p := mpb.New(mpb.WithWidth(defaultTerminalWidth))
bar := p.AddBar(math.MaxInt64, mpb.AppendDecorators(decor.Percentage()))
```

`mpb.New` without `WithOutput` renders to `os.Stdout` — the same stream the presenter writes tables, JSON, and TSV to. The README explicitly advertises `grafaman coverage ... -f json | jq`, and mpb writes refresh frames with cursor-control escapes regardless of whether stdout is a TTY, so piped JSON gets corrupted by progress frames. Worse, nothing ever finishes the bar: the total starts at `math.MaxInt64`, `SetTotal(newTotal, false)` never marks completion, and `p.Wait()` is never called, so the render goroutine is still repainting while the final report is printed, interleaving output. The `ProgressListener` contract (`internal/provider/graphite/contract.go:12`) has no completion hook at all.

**Fix.** Render to stderr (`mpb.WithOutput(os.Stderr)`), disable the bar entirely when stderr is not a terminal, extend the listener contract with a `Done`/`Close` step, mark the bar complete (`SetTotal(n, true)`) and call `p.Wait()` before the presenter prints anything.

## 5. Toolchain, dependencies, CI, and release pipeline are frozen in 2020

`go.mod:3` (plus `.travis.yml:1`, `.golangci.yml:4`, `.goreleaser.yml:10`, `Makefile:5`, `README.md:142`)

Everything about the repo's supply chain predates 2021 and much of it is now dead, not merely old:

- **Toolchain.** `go 1.15` — pre-generics, pre-`//go:build`, pre-embedded VCS info. The `init()` dance in `main.go:30` that stitches `commit` from `debug.ReadBuildInfo` predates Go 1.18 build settings (`vcs.revision`, `vcs.time`) and today prints `unknown, mod sum: ...` for source builds.
- **CI.** Travis CI (`.travis.yml`) is effectively defunct for OSS since late 2021; the build badge in the README is dead. The deploy step `curl -sL https://git.io/goreleaser | bash` is doubly broken: GitHub disabled all `git.io` redirects in 2022, and pipe-to-bash from a link shortener was never a good idea.
- **Release.** The `.goreleaser.yml` schema (`replacements`, `brews.github`, `folder`) was removed in goreleaser v2 — the config no longer parses. `godownloader` (generates `bin/install`) is archived.
- **Lint.** `.golangci.yml` enables `deadcode`, `structcheck`, `varcheck` — all deprecated in 2022 and deleted from golangci-lint; the commented list (`interfacer`, `scopelint`, `golint`, `maligned`) is equally gone; `exportloopref`/`looppointer` are obsolete since Go 1.22 changed loop-variable semantics; the config format itself is now v2.
- **Dependencies.** `github.com/pkg/errors` is archived (std `%w`/`errors.Is` cover it); `github.com/golang/mock` is archived (moved to `go.uber.org/mock`); ginkgo v1 is EOL (v2 since 2021); `mpb/v5` is at v8; `c-bata/go-prompt` v0.2.5 is abandoned with its infamous unrestored-terminal-state bug — a REPL exit can leave the user's terminal broken; `io/ioutil` (`internal/cnf/option.go:73`, `main_test.go:4`) is deprecated. `cobra` v1.1.1 predates the built-in `completion` command.
- **Distribution docs.** `README.md:142` recommends `go get github.com/kamilsk/grafaman@latest`, which stopped installing binaries in Go 1.17; it must be `go install ...@latest`.
- **Missing safety nets.** No `govulncheck`, no Dependabot, no CodeQL, and a committed `vendor/` tree with `GOPROXY=direct` instead of the module proxy + checksum DB.

**Fix.** One modernization pass: bump `go.mod` to a current toolchain and drop `vendor/`; migrate CI to GitHub Actions (test matrix + `golangci-lint` v2 config + `govulncheck` + Dependabot); regenerate `.goreleaser.yml` for v2 and delete `bin/install` in favor of goreleaser-generated artifacts or `go install`; replace pkg/errors with `fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)`, golang/mock with uber-go/mock, ginkgo v1 with v2 (or plain `testing`), mpb/v5 with v8, and go-prompt with a maintained prompt library (e.g. bubbletea/readline); read version info from `debug.ReadBuildInfo().Settings`; fix the README install instructions and badges.

## 6. Cache ignores the last flag and serves mismatched data for a day

`internal/provider/graphite/cache/decorator.go:63` (key: `decorator.go:39`, TTL: `decorator.go:68`)

The cache key is `Filename(prefix)` — the `last` argument participates neither in the key nor in the stored payload, and the TTL is hardcoded to one day regardless of what was asked. Run `grafaman metrics --last 1h`, then `grafaman metrics --last 7d`: the second call returns the cached 1-hour result for up to 24 hours and reports it as 7-day data. There is also no self-healing: a truncated or corrupt cache file makes `json.Decoder.Decode` fail (line 52) and the whole command errors out until the user manually finds and deletes the file — the cache layer turns from an optimization into a hard dependency. Finally, two concurrent runs share one `O_RDWR` file with no locking, so interleaved truncate/write can produce exactly such a corrupt file.

**Fix.** Include `last` (and any other fetch-shaping inputs) in the cache key or in the stored record and compare on read; treat any decode error as a cache miss (log, refetch, overwrite); write atomically via temp-file-plus-rename instead of truncate-in-place to be safe under concurrency.

## 7. Predictable world-readable cache file in the shared temp directory

`internal/provider/graphite/cache/decorator.go:27` and `decorator.go:41`

```go
return filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), prefix) + ".grafaman.json"
```

The cache lives at a fully predictable path in the machine-wide temp directory, created with mode `0644`. On any multi-user host, another local user can pre-create that file (or, depending on the platform, plant a symlink) and thereby feed arbitrary metric lists into someone else's coverage report, or simply read what services and metrics a colleague is analyzing. Data that influences a report's correctness should not be writable by other users.

**Fix.** Move the cache under `os.UserCacheDir()` (e.g. `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/grafaman/<prefix>.json`) with `0600` permissions and create the directory with `0700`. This also survives reboots and temp cleaners more predictably than `/tmp`.

## 8. Config loading swallows read errors and panics on unmarshal errors

`internal/cnf/option.go:46` (switch: `option.go:30`)

The `switch err := cfg.ReadInConfig()` has arms only for `err == nil` and `os.IsNotExist(err)`. A present-but-malformed `.env.paas` (or an unreadable one: permissions, EISDIR) falls through both arms and is silently ignored; the user then gets the misleading "please provide Grafana API endpoint" from `PreRunE` instead of "your config file is broken". The `app.toml` fallback swallows its read error the same way (line 36). Meanwhile every remaining step is wrapped in `fn.Must(...)`, so a type mismatch in `container.Unmarshal(config)` — e.g. an unparsable `GRAPHITE_TIMEOUT` value — panics; `safe.Do` in `main.go` converts that into a "recovered: ..." stack dump and exit 1 rather than a one-line user-facing error. This callback is a `PreRunE` — it has an error return channel designed for exactly this.

**Fix.** Handle the default case of the switch by returning the wrapped read error; replace the `fn.Must` calls inside `WithConfig` with plain `if err := ...; err != nil { return err }`. Reserve panics for programmer errors (flag binding at startup), not for user input.

## 9. Unbounded goroutine fan-out against the Graphite API

`internal/provider/graphite/provider.go:87`

`recursive` starts one goroutine — and one HTTP request — per non-leaf node at every level of the metrics tree, with no concurrency limit. For a prefix with thousands of intermediate nodes this floods the Graphite endpoint with hundreds of simultaneous `/metrics/find` calls, exhausts client sockets, and looks like a DoS to the server team (the 1-second default client timeout then produces spurious failures under its own self-inflicted load). In 2020 bounding this required a semaphore; since then `errgroup` grew `SetLimit` precisely for this shape of code.

**Fix.** Create the group once at the top of the walk with `group.SetLimit(n)` (n≈8–16, possibly a flag) and pass it down the recursion instead of creating a fresh unbounded group per level. This also removes the per-level mutex/slice juggling if children return their own slices that the parent merges after `Wait`.

## 10. Unsafe SliceHeader tricks where plain conversions and generics do

`internal/model/metric.go:24` (also `metric.go:73`, `query.go:29`, `query.go:50`)

```go
header := (*reflect.SliceHeader)(unsafe.Pointer(&src))
if metrics == nil {
    return *(*[]Metric)(unsafe.Pointer(header))
}
```

Four separate `unsafe.Pointer`/`reflect.SliceHeader` incantations exist to avoid copying `[]string` ↔ `[]Metric` and to reuse `sort.Strings`. `reflect.SliceHeader` is deprecated since Go 1.20 and this usage pattern is exactly what the deprecation targets; more importantly the payoff is zero today: `slices.Sort(metrics)` sorts any ordered element type in place with no conversion at all, and the string↔Metric slice conversion, where still needed, is a three-line loop the compiler handles fine at these sizes (thousands of elements, once per invocation of a network-bound CLI). The `Convert` API is also a trap — it mutates the receiver *and* returns it, and `dashboard.go:56` depends on the mutation side effect in a way that reads like a discarded return value.

**Fix.** Delete the unsafe code: implement `Sort` as `slices.Sort` on the defined slice type, and replace `Convert` with an explicit `func ToMetrics([]string) Metrics` loop (or drop it — half the call sites construct slices they control anyway).

## 11. Command tests cover only flag validation and happy paths are empty

`internal/cmd/coverage_test.go:77` (same pattern in `metrics_test.go`, `queries_test.go`, `lookup_test.go`)

```go
When("correct usage", func() {})
```

The ginkgo "integration" suite spins up two `httptest` servers with empty muxes (`integration_test.go:22`) that are never given handlers, and every spec asserts only that missing-flag errors are produced. The success path — fetch, parse, filter, report — is exercised by zero tests at the command level, which is precisely where findings 1–4 of this review live undetected: a wrong `from` parameter, an unchecked 404, a racy fetch, and stdout corruption would all have surfaced with one honest end-to-end spec feeding canned Graphite/Grafana JSON. Provider-level tests exist, but the command wiring (config precedence, cache decoration, presenter selection) is the layer that regressed silently here.

**Fix.** Register fixture handlers on the two `httptest` servers (a small dashboard JSON and a two-level `/metrics/find` tree), then add one happy-path spec per command asserting the rendered output (use `--no-cache` and `-f json` to keep assertions stable). Running the suite with `-race` in CI would additionally catch finding 1.

## 12. Metric validator rejects uppercase names and accepts trailing dots

`internal/model/metric.go:79`

```go
var validator = regexp.MustCompile(`^(?:[0-9a-z-_]+\.?)*$`)
```

Graphite metric path segments are commonly camelCase (`loadAvg`, `memUsage`) and Grafana dashboards at large use uppercase freely, but `PreRunE` in all commands rejects any `-m` prefix containing an uppercase letter with "invalid metric prefix". Conversely the pattern happily accepts the empty string and a trailing dot (`apps.services.`), both of which are not valid prefixes and only avoid trouble because of separate emptiness checks upstream.

**Fix.** Anchor segments explicitly and include uppercase: `^[0-9A-Za-z_-]+(\.[0-9A-Za-z_-]+)*$`. Keep the dedicated empty-string check or fold it into the regexp as shown.

## 13. SkipRaw and SkipDuplicates read as the opposite of what they do

`internal/model/dashboard.go:12` (consumers: `dashboard.go:35`, `dashboard.go:62`, `internal/cmd/queries.go:67`)

`SkipRaw: true` *keeps* the raw values (it skips raw-processing), and `SkipDuplicates: true` *keeps* duplicates (it skips the dedup pass). Both names invert the behavior they gate; the flag wiring in `queries.go` only works because `--raw` and `--allow-duplicates` happen to bind the double negation back to the intended meaning. `coverage.go:104` then sets `SkipDuplicates: false` with no comment, which every future reader will have to decode again. This is a latent-bug generator, not a live bug.

**Fix.** Rename to intent-revealing positives — `KeepRaw`, `AllowDuplicates` (matching the flag names), `Sort`, `UnpackVariables` — and let the zero value be the default behavior.

## 14. TSV output is not actually tab-separated

`internal/presenter/coverage.go:61`

```go
fmt.Fprintln(output, metric.Metric, "\t", strconv.Itoa(metric.Hits))
```

`Fprintln` inserts a space between each operand, so the "TSV" line is `name<space><tab><space>hits` — three whitespace-delimited tokens. Anything that splits strictly on `\t` (awk -F'\t', `cut -f`, spreadsheet import) sees fields with leading/trailing spaces or the wrong field count; the README's `column -t` example only works because it collapses arbitrary whitespace, which also means plain space-containing values would break it. The metrics variant (`internal/presenter/metrics.go:55`) has a single column today, but will grow the same defect the moment a second column appears.

**Fix.** `fmt.Fprintf(output, "%s\t%d\n", metric.Metric, metric.Hits)`.
